tldr: Using reinforcement learning combined with control barrier functions (CBFs), the Unitree G1 humanoid dodges incoming balls using only imperfect depth images from an onboard camera, avoiding contact across all body links without falling over.
hero_caption: Overview of the PAC-MAN pipeline. During training, privileged geometric relationships between the ball and each body link provide whole-body CBF guidance. During real-world deployment, the policy outputs 29-DoF joint position targets using only proprioception and a masked depth image of the ball extracted from an onboard camera.
overview:
For humanoid robots to operate alongside humans, they need to react to incoming airborne threats in fractions of a second and dodge with their whole body without losing balance. However, real-world robots must rely on onboard sensors such as head cameras. These sensors face severe partial observability: flying objects can leave the field of view, and observations are low-resolution and noisy. While control barrier functions (CBFs) are widely used for safety guarantees, they typically require exact, real-time tracking of the incoming obstacle to function properly.

To overcome this, the authors propose PAC-MAN, a framework that closely couples CBF safety guarantees with realistic onboard sensing. During training, the framework uses privileged simulator information to compute distances between all robot links and the ball, injecting this as CBF guidance into reinforcement learning (RL). At deployment time, the policy runs using only a temporal stack of coarse, segmentation-masked depth images of the ball. Furthermore, incorporating an adversarial motion prior (AMP) prevents awkward, unnatural poses—such as merely jerking the pelvis backward—and instead produces dynamic, human-like evasive reflexes such as crouching and side-jumping.

Experiments evaluated policies on a strict benchmark where any contact with any link counts as a failure. A full joint-space CBF performed exceptionally well when given privileged state information, but its performance degraded when relying purely on a fixed onboard camera during training. In contrast, a lightweight Link-CBF, which provides link-wise clearance rewards, proved robust to perceptual imperfections and closely matched a privileged state oracle. When deployed zero-shot to a physical Unitree G1 robot, this Link-CBF policy achieved a 95% dodge success rate across different types of balls.
contributions: Proposed Perception-Aware CBF-RL for humanoids, coupling coarse partial observations from an onboard depth camera with whole-body control barrier functions (CBFs).

Built a rigorous dodgeball benchmark that penalizes contact with any body link, revealing that the optimal barrier formulation depends on perceptual observability (fixed camera, tracking gimbal, or privileged oracle).
Zero-shot transferred a sim-trained Link-CBF policy to a real Unitree G1 humanoid, achieving a 95% evasion success rate against real-world human throws.

sections.heading: Dodging incoming threats: Co-designing perception and safety barriers
sections.summary: Humanoid dodgeball is a safety-critical problem requiring contact avoidance across the entire body while maintaining balance under partial observability and tight sub-second reaction windows. This section outlines the motivation behind PAC-MAN, which embeds control barrier functions (CBFs) during training while deploying on real hardware with only limited onboard vision.
sections.details:
When a humanoid operates in environments with fast-moving objects, it must perceive the threat, decide which limbs or body links might collide, and coordinate whole-body evasion without falling—all in a fraction of a second. While humans naturally track a flying ball with their gaze and dodge fluidly, doing this on a humanoid robot using only onboard cameras is remarkably challenging.

Control barrier functions (CBFs) are a powerful safety tool designed to ensure systems remain within a designated safe set. However, standard CBF mathematics assumes that the obstacle's precise position and velocity are known in real time. On a robot's onboard head camera, this assumption quickly fails: the ball may span only a few pixels near the edge of the field of view or leave the camera's sight entirely. While CBF-RL approaches integrate barrier constraints into RL rewards or loss functions, the policy struggles to internalize complex safety structures if its runtime observations are too sparse and noisy.

To solve this, the authors co-design the threat perception pipeline and barrier formulation. They examine two formulations: a lightweight Link-CBF (link-level clearance rewards) and a stricter Joint-CBF (joint-space projection filter). This lets them test which safety structure works best across varying perceptual fidelity and camera setups. Additionally, because optimizing purely for collision avoidance tends to yield brittle and awkward motions, they introduce an adversarial motion prior (AMP) to guide the policy toward natural, human-like evasive reflexes such as crouching, twisting, and side-stepping.

captions.F1: Real-world perception-aware dodgeball. Relying solely on coarse depth information and a segmentation mask from a head-mounted depth camera, the robot quickly dodges the incoming ball with its entire body, landing cleanly and maintaining upright balance.

sections.heading: Related work: Moving from agile locomotion to dynamic projectile evasion
sections.summary: This work sits at the intersection of RL-based whole-body motion tracking, push recovery, CBF-based safety control, and agile vision-based locomotion such as parkour. Unlike static terrain traversal, dynamic dodging requires accounting for whole-body geometry against high-speed incoming threats under sub-second deadlines.
sections.details:
Related literature spans three primary areas:

- Motion imitation and motion priors:
Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP), which leverage a GAN-style discriminator to reward human-like movements, have become a standard way to encourage natural motion styles in robots. For tasks like dodgeball, where a simple geometric collision penalty does not specify how the robot should twist or crouch, matching reference human dodge clips is a natural fit.

- Vision-based agile locomotion and fast-moving object tasks:
Recent work in quadruped and humanoid parkour has shown impressive leaps over obstacles using onboard depth cameras and elevation maps. However, parkour deals with static terrain, whereas dodgeball involves fast, transient airborne threats. The ball remains visible for less than a second, requiring rapid trajectory estimation and quick evasive coordination across every limb, rather than just choosing footsteps.

- Whole-body collision avoidance and safety control:
Prior research has established push recovery and CBF-based Model Predictive Control (MPC) to guarantee safety mathematically. More recent work incorporates CBF formulations into RL training to avoid heavy online optimization at runtime. PAC-MAN pushes this concept further, investigating how deeply safety barrier structures can be internalized when the policy is constrained to coarse onboard depth vision.

sections.heading: Task definition: A strict rule set with zero tolerance for contact
sections.summary: The task is modeled as a partially observable Markov decision process where the robot must dodge a ball arriving in about 0.6 seconds using only onboard depth and proprioception. Success requires zero contact across all body links, providing a much stricter and more realistic safety standard than tracking pelvic distance alone.
sections.details:
The dodgeball task is formulated as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). Running at a control frequency of 50 Hz, the policy $\pi_\theta$ outputs 29-DoF target joint positions expressed as offsets from a nominal default pose.

To ensure realistic hardware transfer, the runtime observation vector $o_t$ contains only signals readily accessible on the physical platform: a masked depth image $\mathcal{D}_t$, joint positions and velocities, base angular velocity, the projected gravity vector, and the previous action. Crucially, the deployed policy receives no privileged ground-truth ball position or velocity, forcing it to deduce the projectile's trajectory entirely from temporal depth frames.

Incoming balls are thrown from 2 to 3 meters away at angles within $\pm 25^\circ$ relative to the robot's heading. Flight time is roughly 0.6 seconds, giving the humanoid an extremely tight reaction window. Throws are split evenly between downward trajectories aimed at the lower body (requiring side-steps or leg lifts) and flat trajectories targeting the torso or head (requiring crouching or ducking).

For safety evaluation, the authors adopt an "any-link contact" rule. Conventional benchmarks often measure only the clearance to the pelvis, ignoring collisions that brush against hands, elbows, or feet. PAC-MAN treats any contact between the ball and any link as an immediate "hit." Similarly, losing balance or dropping torso height below a threshold counts as a "fall," making the evaluation exceptionally demanding.

sections.heading: PAC-MAN methodology: Unifying barrier guidance, visual inputs, and AMP
sections.summary: During training, privileged geometric states compute whole-body CBF constraints to guide policy learning. The authors compare a lightweight Link-CBF against a projection-based Joint-CBF, combining them with temporally stacked, low-resolution onboard depth images and human AMP rewards.
sections.details:
PAC-MAN relies on an asymmetric actor-critic architecture. The critic accesses privileged simulation data, including the ball's true relative position, velocity, and exact body link kinematics. The actor, however, sees only onboard sensor observations.

Two levels of safety barriers are evaluated:

- Link-CBF (Link-level barrier reward):
Link clearance is defined as $h_i = \|p^b - p_i\| - (\rho^b + \rho_i)$ for each link $i$. For the most threatened link, a penalty reward is applied whenever the barrier condition $\dot{h}_i + \alpha h_i \ge 0$ is violated. Because of the class $\mathcal{K}$ term $\alpha h_i$, this penalty smoothly scales as the threat approaches rather than waiting for an imminent collision. Because this acts solely as a reward term during training, it requires no extra runtime computation or ground-truth ball states on hardware.

- Joint-CBF (Joint-space barrier projection):
In this stricter formulation, the Jacobian $J_{i^\star}$ of the most endangered link produces an affine constraint on the commanded joint velocities. A closed-form projection filter modifies the target joint velocities to respect this constraint. During training, the policy is penalized proportionally to the magnitude of this filtering correction. In addition, an upper-bound configuration called "+filter" runs this projection directly during evaluation using privileged ball states.

For perception, the ball is segmented out of RGB frames, the background depth is pushed to infinity (the far clipping plane), and the resulting masked depth is pooled down to a minimal $16\times 9$ resolution. Stacking four temporally subsampled frames (from $[0, 3, 8, 18]$ steps ago) allows the policy to capture closing speed and lateral movement. Finally, style rewards from an Adversarial Motion Prior (AMP) trained on human mocap clips guide the emergent evasive behaviors toward stable, human-like ducking, crouching, and dodging.

captions.F3: Whole-body link safety shells (barrier geometry) extracted from human evasive motions. During crouches, jumps, and side-steps, the exclusion zones around each link (colored hulls) adapt dynamically, coordinating the entire body to clear the ball's flight path.

sections.heading: Experimental findings: An overly rigid barrier harms performance under limited vision
sections.summary: In simulation, the lightweight Link-CBF outperformed the heavier Joint-CBF when relying on a fixed camera, reaching an 89% success rate during deployment. In zero-shot physical deployment on the Unitree G1, Link-CBF achieved a 95% dodging rate against human throws and handled multiple ball types seamlessly.
sections.details:
Policies were evaluated in a challenging simulation setup where a stationary robot has a 96% hit rate (just a 4% baseline survival rate). Tests were split into two regimes: "Reset" (the robot is reset to its starting position after each throw) and "Deployment" (the robot walks back to its station and recovers balance between consecutive throws).

A crucial insight emerged: the strength of the barrier formulation must match the information provided by the perception system.
- Under a privileged state oracle (where exact ball position and velocity are known), Joint-CBF with an active runtime filter ("+filter") achieved the highest success rates, reaching 98% to 99%.
- However, when constrained to a fixed onboard camera, Joint-CBF without an active filter dropped to 76% in the Deployment regime—performing worse than an unguided baseline policy (86%). Forcing a policy with limited visibility to internalize complex joint-space constraints led to erratic, unnatural dodges.
- In contrast, the lightweight Link-CBF remained remarkably stable under fixed-camera inputs, achieving 90% in Reset and 89% in Deployment, closely matching the privileged oracle (93%). Giving the camera an active ball-tracking gimbal (Gaze) restored Joint-CBF performance to 90%.

Armed with this finding, the fixed-camera Link-CBF policy was deployed zero-shot to a physical Unitree G1 robot. A head-mounted ZED Mini camera fed frames to EfficientTAM to track and segment the ball at approximately 60 Hz, constructing the same $16\times 9$ depth stack used in training to output joint commands at 50 Hz. Across 20 real-world human throws, the robot successfully dodged 19 times without link contact (a 95% success rate). In all successful runs, links maintained a clearance of 5 cm to 1.7 m beyond their safety shells. Switching segmentation targets also allowed the robot to dodge different objects, from foam balls to soccer balls, without retraining.

captions.F4: Emergent whole-body dodging behaviors in simulation (left) and on the real Unitree G1 (right). The rows display crouching (top), dodging left (middle), and dodging right (bottom). The robot actively repositions its limbs and torso based on projectile height, going well beyond simple pelvic translations.

sections.heading: Conclusion and next steps: The path forward for perception-barrier co-design
sections.summary: PAC-MAN combines onboard vision, control barrier functions, and motion priors to achieve dynamic dodgeball reflexes on a real humanoid. Future work includes implementing an active tracking gimbal in hardware and extending static evasion to continuous, walking avoidance.
sections.details:
This study demonstrates that building safe whole-body reflex behaviors under onboard sensing requires "co-designing perception and safety," tailoring barrier complexity to how well the policy can infer external threats. While full joint-space barriers excel when paired with accurate online filters, simpler link-level rewards (Link-CBF) provide far superior robustness when operating under noisy, fixed-camera onboard vision.

Key avenues for future work include deploying the active ball-tracking gimbal mechanism on hardware and building more accurate onboard ball state estimators. Furthermore, while the current system dodges from a stance and walks back to reset, the authors look toward true loco-evasion: ducking and dodging flying obstacles while continuously walking or navigating through an environment.

takeaways: A stronger barrier is not always safer: the barrier formulation (Link-CBF vs. Joint-CBF) must be calibrated to the perceptual observability available to the policy.
Evaluating whole-body safety requires checking all links (any-link contact) rather than just tracking distance to the pelvis.
A temporal stack of extremely coarse, segmented depth images ($16\times 9$) provides sufficient information for sub-second humanoid dodging on real hardware.
Pairing geometric safety barrier rewards with adversarial motion imitation (AMP) produces natural, stable, and practical whole-body dodging reflexes.
limitations: The ball-tracking active gimbal (Gaze) was evaluated only in simulation using oracle tracking and has not yet been implemented on physical hardware.
Current real-world experiments are restricted to dodging from a stationary stance, lacking seamless integration with ongoing dynamic locomotion.
Visual tracking (EfficientTAM) requires manual initialization (such as a mouse click) to track the ball, falling short of fully autonomous threat detection.
